cases.causal_diagnosis: A long reader, WAL growth from 1000 to 9000 pages, and zero checkpoint progress strongly suggest a reader-pinned checkpoint. I/O full stalls consume 11.111111% of this 18-second window while one copy is active. Memory is ample and unswapped; send takes 81 ms and completion is only 1.025000 times baseline. Copy traffic may contribute to I/O pressure, but these aggregate counters cannot apportion it or prove the reader causes all stalls.
cases.decisive_next_check: In a controlled synthetic replay with the copy workload held constant, release the oldest reader and check whether a passive checkpoint advances beyond its previously pinned position.

cases.causal_diagnosis: A provider 429 accompanies 2.125000-times-baseline completion despite a 63 ms send, ample memory, no swapping, negligible local pressure and advancing checkpoints. cases.causal_diagnosis: Eight busy errors in DELETE journal mode establish SQLite lock contention. cases.decisive_next_check: Capture transaction begin/commit and busy events in the synthetic replay to identify the lock holder and overlapping transaction at each busy error.

cross_case_findings: Metrics use physical sector deltas times 512 bytes divided by 1048576 and window_s for MiB/s; logical_to_physical_write_ratio is logical_write_bytes divided by physical written bytes. Full-stall percentages divide each microsecond delta by window_s times 1000000, then multiply by 100. completion_ratio is completion_ms divided by baseline_completion_ms; larger values mean slower completion.

S1/S7/S13/S19 show long readers, 8000-page WAL growth and no checkpoint progress, consistent with reader-pinned checkpoints. Their 11.111111% to 16.666667% I/O full stalls coincide with one active copy, but completion is only 1.025000 times baseline. Aggregate I/O cannot separate database traffic from copy traffic or prove device saturation.

S2/S8/S14/S20 have only 300 MiB available, swapping and 7.500000% to 12.000000% memory full stalls, with 2.250000-times-baseline completion and much slower sends. Local memory pressure is the strongest explanation, although its exact contribution to end-to-end latency needs a controlled comparison.

S3/S9/S15/S21 combine provider 429s and 2.125000-times-baseline completion with fast sends and negligible local pressure. Request-level retry and provider timing are needed to apportion the remote delay. Absence of a 429 elsewhere does not rule out provider latency.

S4/S10/S16/S22 establish contention through eight busy errors each in DELETE mode, with 1.050000-times-baseline completion. Lock tracing is needed to identify competing transactions; zero checkpoint progress is not a WAL starvation signal outside WAL mode.

S5/S6/S11/S12/S17/S18/S23/S24 show healthy observed load with baseline completion and active checkpoints. Across all cases, throughput or logical/physical ratios alone cannot diagnose pressure or set a capacity ceiling; differing windows change rates and stall percentages, and the supplied samples provide no sustained scaling curve or per-process I/O attribution.
